title: Oscar and the Hymn
premise: Folklorist Ines Iversen returns to the village of Hallowmere to record harvest songs, only to find the villagers refuse to sing any hymn twice — because the second singing invites something in. Waiting on her porch is Wren, the imaginary friend she invented at age seven, unchanged by twenty years, who claims he was never imaginary at all but a bargain made on her behalf before she was born. As the harvest moon approaches, Ines uncovers that the village's founding families, including her own, traded a child each generation for prosperity, and that this year the debt falls to her. To survive until sunrise and break the cycle, Ines must sing the forbidden hymn a second time herself — turning the invitation back on what was invited — at the cost of losing Wren forever.
about_author: Beatrix Joubert is the pen name of a former archivist of regional folk music who spent a decade collecting songs from communities that no longer perform them. She writes horror rooted in the belief that every tradition is a contract, and someone always has to pay.

chapters.title: The Songs They Won't Sing Twice
chapters.summary: Ines arrives in Hallowmere with recording equipment and academic confidence. The innkeeper's wife agrees to one song, then goes pale when asked for an encore. POV: Ines. Beat: unease beneath professional excitement.

chapters.title: Porch Light
chapters.summary: At dusk, Ines finds Wren sitting on her porch steps exactly as she left him at seven years old — same patched coat, same crooked smile. He says, 'You came back. You always come back.' POV: Ines. Beat: vertigo between wonder and dread.

chapters.title: What the Archive Says
chapters.summary: Ines digs through county records and finds gaps: children listed as 'gone to kin' every nineteen years, always before harvest. Her own name appears in a 1970s ledger with a red line through it. POV: Ines. Beat: scholarly curiosity curdling into fear.

chapters.title: Wren Remembers Everything
chapters.summary: Wren describes Ines's childhood with impossible precision — including the night she 'stopped needing him.' He insists he didn't leave; she was taken away from him. POV: Ines. Beat: tenderness tangled with suspicion.

chapters.title: The Vicar's Silence
chapters.summary: Ines interviews Reverend Aldous Crane, keeper of the parish hymnal. He confirms the hymn exists — 'The Harvesting' — but refuses to let her see it, saying some pages are 'on loan.' POV: Ines. Beat: institutional obstruction.

chapters.title: Marta Sings Once
chapters.summary: Elderly Marta Kessler, half-lucid, sings 'The Harvesting' for Ines once, beautifully. When Ines raises the recorder again, Marta grips her wrist hard enough to bruise: 'Never twice. Never for anyone.' POV: Ines. Beat: first real terror.

chapters.title: Nineteen Years
chapters.summary: Ines maps the disappearances: 1951, 1970, 1989, 2008. Next due: this autumn. She realizes she is exactly the right age. Wren watches her do the math and doesn't deny it. POV: Ines. Beat: cold clarity.

chapters.title: The Founding Families
chapters.summary: Research reveals four founding surnames whose descendants still run the village: Iversen among them. Each generation, one child from the four lines was 'given to the field.' POV: Ines. Beat: betrayal by bloodline.

chapters.title: Wren's First Lie
chapters.summary: Ines catches Wren in a contradiction about the night they met. He admits he was sent — but claims he refused his task and chose to be her friend instead. POV: Ines. Beat: heartbreak and doubt.

chapters.title: The Field at Night
chapters.summary: Ines follows a procession of silent villagers to the stubble field, where they stand facing the treeline without speaking. Something vast breathes back at them from the dark. POV: Ines. Beat: communal horror.

chapters.title: Crane's Confession, Partial
chapters.summary: Reverend Crane, drunk, tells Ines the hymn isn't a prayer — it's a summons, sung once to call the thing, once to bind it. The second verse was torn out in 1932. POV: Ines. Beat: the rules take shape.

chapters.title: What Was Invited In
chapters.summary: Crane reveals the truth: in 1932 the village sang the hymn twice by accident, binding the entity instead of banishing it. Every debt since is interest on that mistake. POV: Ines. Beat: the scale of the sin revealed.

chapters.title: Marta's Warning
chapters.summary: Marta lucidly tells Ines that the entity wears the shape you love best — that's how it collects. Ines looks at Wren differently that night. POV: Ines. Beat: poisoned trust.

chapters.title: The Village Turns
chapters.summary: The founding families learn Ines has been asking questions. Shops close to her; her car tires are slashed. The message is clear: come quietly or don't come at all. POV: Ines. Beat: isolation.

chapters.title: Wren Defends Her
chapters.summary: Someone breaks into Ines's room at night. Wren is already there, standing over the intruder, who flees screaming at whatever he saw. Wren's shadow is wrong on the wall. POV: Ines. Beat: gratitude laced with fear.

chapters.title: The Torn Page
chapters.summary: Ines finds the missing second verse hidden in Marta's sewing box, embroidered in thread: instructions not for summoning but for un-inviting. It requires the invited one's consent. POV: Ines. Beat: hope with a terrible price tag.

chapters.title: Consent
chapters.summary: Ines understands: to send it back, the entity must agree to go — and it will only agree if the one who invited it releases it willingly. But who invited it? Not her. Someone else. POV: Ines. Beat: the puzzle deepens.

chapters.title: Her Mother's Ledger
chapters.summary: Ines finds her late mother's diary: her mother tried to substitute herself for baby Ines in 1989 and failed. The last entry reads: 'It keeps him. It calls him Wren too.' POV: Ines. Beat: grief reframes everything.

chapters.title: Wren Is the Debt
chapters.summary: Ines confronts Wren: he isn't her imaginary friend or her protector — he is the collateral, the child given in 1970, kept young and shapeless in the field's keeping. He weeps. POV: Ines. Beat: devastating revelation.

chapters.title: The Harvest Moon Rises
chapters.summary: The moon swells full and orange. The whole village gathers at the field's edge, and the founding families begin to sing 'The Harvesting' — once. The ground answers. POV: Ines. Beat: point of no return.

chapters.title: Taken to the Field
chapters.summary: Villagers escort Ines to the field's center, gentle and terrible, like mourners. The entity rises from the soil wearing her mother's face, then Wren's, then her own. POV: Ines. Beat: abject terror.

chapters.title: The Bargain Offered
chapters.summary: The entity offers Ines the old deal: walk into the earth willingly and Hallowmere prospers another nineteen years — and Wren goes free. Duty dressed as mercy. POV: Ines. Beat: temptation.

chapters.title: Sunrise Deadline
chapters.summary: Wren whispers the escape clause: the binding can be undone before sunrise if the hymn is sung twice by the one who holds the debt — and the second singing must be given, not forced. POV: Ines. Beat: a plan forms against the clock.

chapters.title: Crane's Last Verse
chapters.summary: Ines begs Crane for help; he refuses, then relents, giving her the true final line of the hymn he's memorized in secret for fifty years, waiting for someone brave enough. POV: Ines. Beat: unexpected ally.

chapters.title: The Village Chooses
chapters.summary: Ines stands before the assembled villagers and tells them everything: the ledgers, the children, the 1932 mistake. Some turn away. A few — Marta, the innkeeper's wife — step forward to stand with her. POV: Ines. Beat: justice outside the law begins.

chapters.title: They Come for Marta
chapters.summary: The founding families silence Marta permanently; she is found in the field, smiling, empty. Her death is ruled natural. Ines records the lie on tape and vows to make it evidence. POV: Ines. Beat: rage and resolve.

chapters.title: Documentation Is a Prayer
chapters.summary: Ines spends the day recording testimony from frightened villagers, building an archive that will outlive her whether she does or not. Wren sits beside her, fading at the edges. POV: Ines. Beat: quiet defiance.

chapters.title: Wren Fades
chapters.summary: As the moon nears fullness, Wren grows translucent — the entity reclaiming its collateral. He asks Ines not to save him if saving him means staying bound. POV: Ines. Beat: love against duty crystallizes.

chapters.title: The First Singing
chapters.summary: Midnight. The founding families complete the hymn's first singing at the field. The earth opens like a throat. Ines runs for the center with the embroidered verse in her fist. POV: Ines. Beat: sprint toward doom.

chapters.title: Held Until Sunrise
chapters.summary: The entity traps Ines in a loop of remembered childhoods, offering her endless warm versions of her life with Wren. She clings to the recorded truth on her recorder, playing Marta's voice to break the spell. POV: Ines. Beat: psychological siege.

chapters.title: The Second Singing Begins
chapters.summary: Hours before dawn, Ines stands in the opened field and begins the hymn's second singing alone, voice cracking, while the founding families scream at her to stop. POV: Ines. Beat: courage at its rawest.

chapters.title: The Entity Refuses
chapters.summary: The entity, wearing Wren's face, begs Ines to stop — claims it only ever wanted to be loved, to be kept. The hymn falters. Ines nearly lowers the recorder. POV: Ines. Beat: the cruelest test.

chapters.title: Given, Not Forced
chapters.summary: Ines understands the final condition: she must release Wren willingly — give him up — for the un-inviting to work. She tells him she loves him and lets him choose. POV: Ines. Beat: sacrifice offered freely.

chapters.title: Wren Chooses
chapters.summary: Wren takes her hand, thanks her for inventing him, and speaks his consent to return to the earth. His voice joins hers in the hymn, harmonizing across seventy years. POV: Ines. Beat: grief transfigured into grace.

chapters.title: Un-Invited
chapters.summary: The second singing completes. The field closes. The entity unravels like smoke drawn backward, taking the false warmth with it. Dawn bleeds gray over Hallowmere. POV: Ines. Beat: climax resolves into exhausted stillness.

chapters.title: Aftermath at Sunrise
chapters.summary: The founding families stand ruined in daylight as Ines plays the recordings aloud — testimonies, ledgers, Marta's voice. Outside the law, she delivers them to judgment: exposure, archive, memory. POV: Ines. Beat: justice rendered.

chapters.title: The Village Without the Debt
chapters.summary: Weeks later, Hallowmere is poorer and freer. Children play in the field. The innkeeper's wife sings a song twice, badly, laughing. POV: Ines. Beat: fragile renewal.

chapters.title: The Last Recording
chapters.summary: Ines catalogs her tapes and labels the final one simply 'Wren.' She plays it once — his voice singing harmony — then locks it away, refusing to listen twice. POV: Ines. Beat: mourning with discipline.

chapters.title: A Porch, Empty
chapters.summary: Ines leaves Hallowmere. On the last morning she checks the porch out of habit. Nothing waits there, and the nothing is its own kind of answer. POV: Ines. Beat: acceptance.

chapters.title: Coda: What the Archive Keeps
chapters.summary: Years on, a folklorist requests the Iversen Collection and finds a hymn with two verses and a note: 'Sing it once, and remember. Never twice.' The songs survive; so does the warning. POV: archival frame. Beat: the story becomes folklore itself.
